# 0007: Skills distribution per OS

Status: Accepted. Several behaviors are unverified and marked so.

## Decision

The source of truth for shared skills is `<config-dir>/skills/<name>/` (0003). Each skill is made visible to each tool by one `Link` op per skill and per target directory (never by replacing a whole skills directory), so the tool only ever owns entries it created and user-made skills next to them are untouched.

| OS | Default method | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Windows | directory junction | needs no administrator rights or developer mode (verified in the prototype this design comes from) |
| Linux | symlink | standard |
| macOS | symlink | standard |

Fallback order when a link cannot be created or a tool does not follow links:

1. **Link** (junction or symlink).
2. **Copy plus manifest** (`allow_copy_fallback`): copy the folder, write a small marker file inside it with the source hash so `status` can detect drift and `sync` can refresh it. Where the tool needs its own manifest of skills, the adapter plans the edit of that manifest as an ordinary `EditFile` op.
3. Report the skill as not distributable for that tool. Never fail silently.

Per tool:

- **Antigravity** (refined by 0013: one `skills.json` entry per skill, pointing at the source folder, with no link and no copy, on every OS): does not follow Windows junctions (known), so on Windows it uses copy plus manifest. On Linux and macOS it also uses copy plus manifest until symlink-following is verified (unverified; this is the safe default, not a finding).
- **Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode**: link in each tool's skills directory. Tools that read the shared agents skills directory are linked there once; the engine de-duplicates link targets across adapters.

Rules that make it safe:

- Ownership: a destination that already exists and is not recorded in the ledger is a conflict. It is reported and left alone; it is never overwritten or deleted.
- Undo (0005) records the `before` state of each destination (`absent`, an existing link and its target, or an existing directory). Removing a copied tree on undo requires its hash to match the recorded one.
- Name collisions between a source skill and a skill already in a target directory are conflicts, shown in the plan.

## Reason

- Per-skill links make `sync` additive and reversible, and protect skills the user installed by other means.
- Junctions are the one Windows link type that works without privileges for directories; symlinks need privileges there.
- A copy fallback is the only method that works for a tool that ignores links, at the price of needing a drift check.

## Verification plan

The maintainer has no Mac. Verification is therefore split by what can actually be run:

1. **Windows**: on the maintainer's machine, with the real tools.
2. **Linux**: through WSL on the same machine, with the real tools installed there. This covers symlink-following for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Antigravity, and the Antigravity manifest question, on Linux.
3. **macOS**: only through GitHub Actions macOS runners, and only for what runs there without a login: the unit and contract tests, and the link, atomic-write and path logic against fixtures. Anything that needs a real, signed-in tool on macOS is **not verified**.
4. Everything not verified by 1 to 3 stays marked "unverified" in the adapter docstring, in this ADR and in the support table of the README. Nothing is promoted to "supported" on a guess.

## Open points (unverified)

- Whether Codex, OpenCode and Claude Code follow symlinks to skill folders on Linux and macOS. Believed yes; not checked. Needs a real-tool check on each OS before v0.1 is announced.
- Whether Antigravity follows symlinks on Linux or macOS, and whether it needs its manifest there. Not checked.
- Which tools read the shared agents skills directory is a convention observed in the prototype, not a guarantee; each adapter's `paths()` must state its source and be re-checked per release.
- Junction creation uses either `_winapi.CreateJunction` (undocumented in the standard library) or `mklink /J`; pick one in the implementation and test both Python versions in CI.
- Windows file-system limits (long paths) when copying deep skill trees.

# one-setup-all-agents

**One setup for all your AI coding agents.** A shared agent config for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Antigravity: write your config once, every agent gets the same setup, and any change can be undone with one command.

> **Status: pre-alpha.** The four public commands (`init`, `sync`, `status`, `undo`) are implemented with full engine safety guarantees (atomic writes, journaled operations, backups, and undo). Real-world verification against live tool environments is in progress. Do not install it expecting a finished production release.

## Why

If you use more than one AI coding agent, you keep the same things in several places: your global instructions, your MCP servers, your skills. Each tool stores them in a different file with a different format, and they drift apart. Syncing them by hand is tedious, and a sync tool that rewrites your real config files is scary.

`one-setup-all-agents` is built around the second problem. It does not try to support the most tools. It tries to be the one you trust with your real config:

- **Write once.** One source config; every detected tool gets the same instructions, MCP servers and skills.
- **Safe by default.** `sync` shows a dry run first. Every write is atomic, backed up and recorded.
- **Undo with one command.** `all-agents undo` reverses the last change, from one journal that covers every kind of change.
- **Nothing to trust blindly.** Zero runtime dependencies (Python standard library only). Secrets are referenced by environment-variable name; their values are never read, printed or stored.

## Quick Start (5 minutes)

Try it in dry-run mode without installing:

```bash
uvx one-setup-all-agents init --dry-run
```

Or install with `pipx`:

```bash
pipx install one-setup-all-agents
```

### 1. Import your existing setup

Detect your installed tools and import existing instructions, MCP servers, and skills into the shared config:

```bash
all-agents init
```

Expected output:
```text
Detected tools:
  Claude Code (claude): installed (~/.claude)
  Codex (codex): installed (~/.codex)
Import proposal:
  - Instructions: imported
  - MCP servers (2): imported
  - Skills (1): imported
initialised operation 20261110T024601Z-71bf
the safety snapshot is kept permanently
```

### 2. Review and apply changes to all agents

Preview the planned changes across all tools, then confirm to apply:

```bash
all-agents sync
```

Expected output:
```text
Plan: 2 change(s), 0 conflict(s)
To run:
  1. edit file ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md: write the shared instructions
  2. edit file ~/.codex/AGENTS.md: write the shared instructions
Apply these changes? [y/N]: y
applied operation 20261110T024601Z-3b2f
```

### 3. Verify that all agents match

Check the status of every tool and kind of configuration:

```bash
all-agents status
```

Expected output:
```text
Claude Code (claude): in sync
  instructions: in sync
  mcp: in sync
  skills: in sync
Codex (codex): in sync
  instructions: in sync
  mcp: in sync
  skills: in sync
Undoable operations: 2
```

### 4. Reverse any change if needed

Undo the last operation with exact byte or CLI inversion from the journal:

```bash
all-agents undo
```

Expected output:
```text
undone operation 20261110T024601Z-3b2f (sync)
1 more can be undone
```

## Config Locations

Source configuration and engine state locations follow standard platform conventions (see [ADR 0002](docs/decisions/0002-config-and-state-locations.md)):

| OS | Shared Config (`config_dir`) | Engine State (`state_dir`) |
|---|---|---|
| Windows | `%APPDATA%/one-setup-all-agents` | `%LOCALAPPDATA%/one-setup-all-agents` |
| Linux | `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/one-setup-all-agents` (or `~/.config/...`) | `$XDG_STATE_HOME/one-setup-all-agents` (or `~/.local/state/...`) |
| macOS | `~/.config/one-setup-all-agents` | `~/.local/state/one-setup-all-agents` |

Overrides: Setting `ALL_AGENTS_CONFIG_DIR` or `ALL_AGENTS_STATE_DIR` overrides the default paths on all operating systems.

## How Secrets Work

`one-setup-all-agents` operates under a zero-secret-exposure principle:

- **Variable References Only:** Secrets (API keys, tokens, auth headers) are referenced strictly by environment-variable name (e.g. `${GITHUB_TOKEN}` or `Authorization: Bearer <NAME>`).
- **No Secret Values:** Cleartext secret values are never requested, read from your environment, printed to stdout/stderr, written to disk, or stored in journals or backups.
- **CLI Guard:** If an adapter must run an external CLI (such as `claude mcp add-json`), arguments are scanned to ensure no secret values are passed on the process command line.

## Safety Model

`one-setup-all-agents` is designed to be the tool you trust with your real developer environment:

- **Dry-run by default:** `sync` shows a detailed change plan before asking for confirmation.
- **Atomic file writes:** Config files are written using temporary siblings and atomic replacements; incomplete writes never corrupt your setup.
- **Private permissions:** State directories are created with `0700` and journal files with `0600` on POSIX systems.
- **Automatic backups:** Every modified file is backed up before any write occurs.
- **Unified journal:** All operations (file edits, links, CLI calls) are recorded with exact inverse actions in an append-only journal.
- **Drift detection:** `undo` checks that file contents match what was written. If you edited a file manually after running `sync`, `undo` refuses to overwrite your manual changes unless `--force` is specified.
- **What undo does not promise:** External edits made outside `all-agents` cannot be anticipated, and processes terminated abruptly during external CLI invocations must be inspected manually.

## Known Boundaries & Limits

- **Antigravity HTTP headers:** Antigravity does not support environment-variable expansion in HTTP headers; remote MCP servers requiring authorization headers are flagged as unsupported and skipped.
- **Windows Junctions:** Antigravity does not follow directory junctions; skills are referenced by direct directory paths in `skills.json`.
- **Codex Overrides:** If a non-empty `AGENTS.override.md` is present in Codex config, `all-agents` flags a conflict rather than silently writing inactive instructions.
- **Claude Code CLI:** Claude Code configuration is maintained through `claude mcp` CLI calls to avoid race conditions with running Claude sessions. Parameters not supported by the CLI (like `cwd`) are flagged as unsupported.

## Roadmap

- **v0.1**: The four public commands (`init`, `sync`, `status`, `undo`), global scope, for instructions, MCP servers, and skills.
- **v0.2**: Project scope, including safety and permissions for shared repositories you do not own.
- **Later**: Hooks, granular tool permissions, memory, and accounts.

## Adding a tool adapter

The architecture has one rule: **adapters detect, read and plan; they never write.** Only `engine/` writes files, backs them up, journals them and undoes them. That is what makes `undo` work the same for every tool. Read `docs/decisions/0008-adapter-engine-boundary.md` first. For a complete step-by-step walkthrough, see `docs/adding-a-tool.md`.

A new tool is:

1. **`src/one_setup_all_agents/adapters/<tool>.py`**: a subclass of `ToolAdapter` with a unique `id`, a `label` and the `capabilities` it supports. Implement:
   - `detect(env)`: is the tool installed, where is its binary and config, which version.
   - `paths(env, scope)`: where it keeps instructions, MCP servers and skills, per OS. Honor the tool's own override variables.
   - `read_instructions`, `read_mcp`, `read_skills`: what is configured now.
   - `plan_instructions`, `plan_mcp`, `plan_skills`: pure functions that return `Op` objects (`EditFile`, `RunCli`, `Link`). Touch only entries the tool owns (the `owned` argument, a `frozenset` of item keys: server names, skill names, or `instructions`). List the items an op creates in `claims` and the ones it removes in `releases`. Report an existing, unowned entry that is in the way as a `Conflict` instead of writing. Every `RunCli` needs an inverse command.
   - Kinds the tool cannot express need no code: the base class reports them as `Unsupported` so the plan shows the gap.
   - If the tool cannot store a field of the neutral model, override `normalize_mcp` (or `normalize_instructions`) to say exactly which.
   - `notes()`: known limits worth showing to the user.
   - `import_notes(env, scope)`: optional notes on unimported secrets or settings during initialisation.
   - `snapshot_files(env, scope)`: existing files of this tool to preserve in the safety snapshot before writes.
2. **A registry entry** in `adapters/__init__.py`: one import line and one entry in the `ADAPTERS` tuple. Nothing else in that file changes.
3. **A fixture**: a fake home directory with the tool's config files, under `tests/fixtures/`. Use neutral names (`example`, `demo-server`); no real paths, users or secrets.
4. **The contract test** must pass for the adapter (`docs/decisions/0008` and `0009`). It is `tests/adapter_contract.py`, a reusable mixin, and `tests/test_adapter_contract.py` already creates a test class that runs the full suite for every adapter in `ADAPTERS`. Add a seed function for your fixture home to `REGISTERED_SEEDS` in that file only if the home should start with the user's own config (and a `REGISTERED_EXTRAS` entry only if your adapter plans `RunCli` ops or needs a different `make_env`, `unwritten_mcp` or `removable_mcp`). The suite checks, in a temporary home: reading what a plan produces returns the desired state (after the adapter's `normalize_*`), a second plan is empty, `plan_*` and `read_*` write nothing, entries that are not owned are left alone (a clash is a `Conflict`), owned entries that leave the source are removed, `paths()` stays under the given `Env`, every kind outside `capabilities` plans as `Unsupported`, every `RunCli` has an inverse, and undo restores the original bytes. Run it with `python -m unittest discover -s tests` (or `python -m unittest test_adapter_contract` from `tests/`). The suite applies and undoes your ops with the real engine (`tests/contract_applier.py`, one seam: `make_applier`, which calls `engine/`): journal, backups, atomic writes, drift check and ledger. A pass shows that, in a temporary home on the OS the tests run on, your ops are undone to the exact bytes, permission bits, links and ownership. **Caveat:** it does not prove anything about the real tool (where it keeps files, whether it follows links, what a real CLI does) or the `undo` command itself (which is tested separately in `tests/test_cmd_undo.py` and `tests/test_undo_matrix.py`); `docs/decisions/0010-engine-v1.md` lists what is and is not proven.
5. **Nothing else changes.** You do not edit `engine/`, `model.py`, `cli.py`, `adapters/base.py`, `adapters/_common.py` or another adapter. Two tests hold you to it:
   - `tests/test_tool_boundary.py` scans every source file outside the adapter modules (and `_core/`, which holds internal shared utilities: formatting, masking, runner) and fails if one names a tool, its id or label, or a tool's config file name. If you need something the engine or base class does not offer, add a generic hook with a default to `adapters/base.py` instead of a special case, and keep the other adapters' behavior unchanged.
   - `tests/test_drop_in_tool.py` adds a made-up tool (`tests/demo_tool_adapter.py`, one module) with a patched registry and shows that it is found, planned, applied and undone next to the four real tools without touching their files, that every op it plans lies under its own config folder, and that the contract suite runs for it. Use that module as a template.
6. **Unverified behavior is labeled.** If you could not check a file location or a behavior on one OS, say so in the adapter docstring and in the ADR, rather than guessing.

# Security Policy

## Supported Versions

`one-setup-all-agents` is currently in pre-alpha / active development. While pre-1.0, security updates and bug fixes are provided for the latest released version only.

| Version | Supported |
|---|---|
| Latest release (`>=0.0.0`) | :white_check_mark: |
| Older releases | :x: |

## Reporting a Vulnerability

If you discover a security vulnerability or potential data leak in `one-setup-all-agents`, please report it privately through GitHub's Private Vulnerability Reporting:

**[Report a vulnerability via GitHub Advisory](https://github.com/beingmomen/one-setup-all-agents/security/advisories/new)**

Do **not** open a public issue or discussion for an unpatched vulnerability.

### Response Timeline
- **Acknowledgment:** We aim to acknowledge reports within 7 days.
- **Resolution or Explanation:** We aim to provide a fix or public explanation within 90 days.
- **Capacity:** Project maintenance is currently carried out on a best-effort basis by a single maintainer.

### What to Include
When submitting a report, please include:
- The exact version of `one-setup-all-agents` and Python version (`all-agents --version` and `python --version`).
- Operating system and version (Windows, Linux distro, macOS).
- Clear, minimal step-by-step reproduction instructions.
- A proof-of-concept configuration or demonstration where possible.
- **Never include real secrets, tokens, or credentials in your report.** Use dummy placeholders (e.g. `MOCK_SECRET_TOKEN`).

## In Scope and Out of Scope

### In Scope
- Any behavior causing `one-setup-all-agents` to read, print to logs/terminal, or persist cleartext secrets.
- Writes or modifications made outside the items explicitly owned or configured by `all-agents`.
- Loss or corruption of user configuration files upon running `all-agents undo`.
- Unintended or malicious command execution triggered during configuration processing.
- Path traversal vulnerabilities in journal logging, backups, snapshot extraction, or history pruning.
- Supply chain security vulnerabilities in packaging or distribution artifacts.

### Out of Scope
- Attacks requiring prior root, administrator, or privileged local machine compromise.
- Attacks relying on social engineering or physical access to the device.
- Unsupported operating systems or modified/forked engine versions.
- Bugs that do not breach confidentiality, file safety boundaries, or execution integrity.

## Security Model

`one-setup-all-agents` is built around safety and least privilege:

1. **Zero Secret Storage:**
   - Secrets are referenced strictly by environment-variable name (e.g. `${GITHUB_TOKEN}` or `Authorization: Bearer <NAME>`).
   - Secret-like values are detected and masked using pattern detectors implemented in `src/one_setup_all_agents/_core/mask.py` and filtered during plan rendering in `src/one_setup_all_agents/engine/plan.py`.
2. **Subprocess Isolation:**
   - When tool detection runs version probes or external adapter CLIs are executed, commands are invoked directly as argument vectors without a shell (`shell=False`), preventing shell injection attacks.
   - Enforced in `src/one_setup_all_agents/detect.py` and `src/one_setup_all_agents/engine/runcli.py`.
3. **Atomic Writes and File Permissions:**
   - All file modifications are staged through temporary files and applied atomically.
   - Files are written with restricted permissions (`0600` for sensitive files, `0700` for state directories on POSIX systems).
   - Enforced in `src/one_setup_all_agents/engine/atomic.py` and `src/one_setup_all_agents/engine/fsops.py`.
4. **Safety Backups and Reversible Journal:**
   - Before any file edit or link change is performed, a full byte backup is captured in the engine state directory.
   - Enforced in `src/one_setup_all_agents/engine/backup.py`.
   - Backups are never printed and cannot be read without local user permissions.
5. **Zero Runtime Dependencies:**
   - The runtime relies exclusively on the Python standard library, eliminating third-party dependency vulnerabilities.
6. **Data Guardrails:**

# Guide to Adding a New Tool Adapter

This guide walks you through adding a new tool adapter to `one-setup-all-agents`.

Before starting, read `docs/decisions/0008-adapter-engine-boundary.md` and `docs/decisions/0009-adapter-interface-v1.md`.

## The Core Rule: Separation of Concerns

The central architectural rule of this project is:

> **Adapters detect, read and plan. They never write.**

Only the `engine/` package writes files, takes backups, manages locks, writes journals, and executes undos. Because adapters only plan operations (`Op` objects) rather than executing them, every tool gets atomic updates, backup snapshots, drift protection, and complete multi-step undo for free.

## Prerequisites

- Python 3.11 or newer.
- No new runtime dependencies: all adapter logic must rely exclusively on the Python standard library.
- Neutral fixtures: test fixtures must never contain real user paths, personal usernames, real tokens, or machine-dependent paths.
- Two boundary tests protect this architecture:
  - `tests/test_tool_boundary.py`: static boundary test asserting that no file outside `adapters/` (and its tests) references any concrete tool id, label, or tool-specific configuration file.
  - `tests/test_drop_in_tool.py`: dynamic boundary test proving that an adapter can be added in a single module without touching engine or model code.
  - See `tests/demo_tool_adapter.py` for a complete reference implementation of a drop-in adapter.

## The ToolAdapter Contract

Every adapter inherits from `ToolAdapter` (in `src/one_setup_all_agents/adapters/base.py`).

### Required Class Attributes

- `id`: A unique, short lowercase identifier used in CLI arguments and journal ledgers (e.g. `"demo-tool"`).
- `label`: A human-readable display name (e.g. `"Demo Tool"`).
- `capabilities`: A `frozenset[Kind]` listing the configuration kinds this tool can express (`Kind.INSTRUCTIONS`, `Kind.MCP`, `Kind.SKILLS`).

### Discovery Methods

- `detect(env)`: Abstract method. Checks whether the tool is installed in `env` and returns a `Detection` object containing installation status, configuration directory roots, and any detection warnings. It is strictly read-only and never spawns processes.
- `version_probe(env, binary)`: Declares how to probe the binary's version without executing it directly during detection. Defaults to `VersionProbe((str(binary), "--version"), parse_version)`. Return `None` if running the tool has unavoidable side effects.
- `paths(env, scope)`: Abstract method. Returns a `Paths` dataclass containing the locations of instructions, MCP configuration, settings, and skills directory for the given `Scope` (e.g. global). All paths must be derived from `env.home` or `env.environ`; never query the host operating system directly.

### Reading Methods

- `read_instructions(env, scope)`: Abstract method. Reads and returns the current `Instructions` file (with `path` and decoded `text`), or `None` if absent.
- `read_mcp(env, scope)`: Abstract method. Reads the tool's configured MCP servers into a dictionary `{name: McpServer}`, including any unowned user servers.
- `read_skills(env, scope)`: Abstract method. Reads the skills visible to the tool, returning a list of `SkillRef`.
- `snapshot_files(env, scope)`: Returns a tuple of existing configuration file paths to preserve in the safety backup snapshot prior to any writes. Defaults to paths for instructions, MCP, and settings.
- `import_notes(env, scope)`: Returns a list of `ImportNote` items describing unimported secrets or unsupported settings during initialisation. Defaults to an empty list.

### Planning Methods

- `plan_instructions(env, scope, desired, owned)`: Abstract method. Compares `desired` instructions against the current state and returns `Op` objects. If the file exists and is unowned, return a `Conflict`.
- `plan_mcp(env, scope, desired, owned)`: Abstract method. Compares desired MCP servers against current servers, updating only owned entries. Returns `Op` objects (e.g. `EditFile` or `RunCli`).
- `plan_skills(env, scope, desired, owned)`: Abstract method. Compares desired skills against current skills and returns `Link` ops linking or unlinking skill directories.
- `wanted_links(env, scope, desired)`: Returns `WantedLink` descriptors for skill links this adapter desires, preventing premature deletion when multiple tools share a common directory.
- `plan_hooks(env, scope, desired, owned)`: Hook planning for future releases. Default returns an `Unsupported` op.
- `plan_permissions(env, scope, desired, owned)`: Permission planning for future releases. Default returns an `Unsupported` op.
- `plan_memory(env, scope, desired, owned)`: Memory planning for future releases. Default returns an `Unsupported` op.

### Normalization and Documentation

- `normalize_instructions(text)`: Normalizes instruction text to match what survives a write and read cycle. Defaults to returning `text` unchanged.
- `normalize_mcp(servers)`: Normalizes desired `McpServer` mappings by stripping fields the tool's format cannot store (e.g. resetting `startup_timeout_sec=None`). Anything not explicitly stripped must survive round-trip tests.
- `notes()`: Returns a list of strings documenting known limits or quirks of the tool displayed by `status`.

## Operation Rules

When planning operations, every adapter must adhere to the following rules:

1. **Claims and Releases**:
   - Every state-modifying op (`EditFile`, `RunCli`, `Link`) must set `claims` for items it creates or updates, and `releases` for items it removes.
   - Items are referenced by `ItemRef(adapter.id, kind, item_key)`.
   - The engine ledger uses these to track ownership.
2. **Mandatory Inverse for CLI Commands**:
   - Every `RunCli` operation must specify `inverse_argv`.
   - Without an inverse command, the engine cannot undo changes.
3. **Conflict Over Overwrite**:
   - Never overwrite existing, unowned configuration. If a user already created a server or file that differs from `desired`, yield a `Conflict` op instead of replacing it.

## Testing and Contract Suite

### Reusable Contract Suite

Every adapter is tested against `tests/adapter_contract.py`. To plug into the contract test runner:

- `REGISTERED_SEEDS`: In `tests/test_adapter_contract.py`, map your adapter id to a seed function `seed_home(env)` that creates initial fixture files (e.g. the user's own native config before `all-agents`).
- `REGISTERED_EXTRAS`: Optional mapping in `tests/test_adapter_contract.py` from adapter id to a function returning extra members for its contract class (the hooks `make_env` and `make_cli` of `AdapterContract`, needed by an adapter that plans `RunCli` ops).
- `unwritten_mcp`: Hook returning names of harness desired MCP servers that this adapter deliberately does not write (defaults to `frozenset()`).
- `removable_mcp`: Hook specifying the name of an MCP server to delete during the removal test (defaults to `"demo-remote"`).

## Registering the Adapter

Once your adapter class is implemented, register it in `src/one_setup_all_agents/adapters/__init__.py`:

1. Import your adapter class (e.g. `from .demo_tool import DemoToolAdapter`).
2. Add the adapter class to the `ADAPTERS` tuple:

```python
from .demo_tool import DemoToolAdapter

ADAPTERS: tuple[type[ToolAdapter], ...] = (
    # ...,
    DemoToolAdapter,
)
```

Adding the adapter to `ADAPTERS` in `adapters/__init__.py` automatically exposes it to discovery, reading, planning, CLI help text generation, and the boundary tests.

### Platform Behavior Rule

Always label unverified platform behavior. If a file location or CLI option is not confirmed by a live test on a given operating system (Windows, Linux, macOS), state that it is unverified in your docstrings, in `notes()`, and in the accompanying decision record. Never guess platform behaviors.

### Planning MCP with Conflict Detection

<!-- excerpt: tests/demo_tool_adapter.py -->
```python
def plan_mcp(
    self, env: Env, scope: Scope, desired: Mapping[str, McpServer], owned: Owned
) -> list[Op]:
    path = self.paths(env, scope).mcp
    old = path.read_bytes() if path.is_file() else None
    current = _raw_servers(path)
    ops: list[Op] = []
    upserts: dict[str, dict] = {}
    for name, server in desired.items():
        entry = _encode(server)
        if current.get(name) == entry:
            continue
        if name in current and name not in owned:
            reason = "an MCP server with this name exists and was not created by all-agents"
            ops.append(Conflict(self.id, Kind.MCP, name, reason, path))
            continue
        upserts[name] = entry
    removals = [n for n in sorted(owned - desired.keys()) if n in current]
    if upserts or removals:
        ops.append(self._edit(path, old, upserts, removals))
    return ops


def normalize_mcp(self, servers: Mapping[str, McpServer]) -> dict[str, McpServer]:
    return {n: replace(s, startup_timeout_sec=None) for n, s in servers.items()}
```

# 0002: Config and state locations per OS

Status: Accepted (macOS follows Linux, confirmed by the maintainer)

## Decision

Two separate directories, both created on demand, both overridable.

| | Config directory (the user's source of truth) | State directory (machine-local: journal, backups, lock) |
|---|---|---|
| Windows | `%APPDATA%\one-setup-all-agents` | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\one-setup-all-agents` |
| Linux | `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/one-setup-all-agents`, default `~/.config/one-setup-all-agents` | `$XDG_STATE_HOME/one-setup-all-agents`, default `~/.local/state/one-setup-all-agents` |
| macOS | `~/.config/one-setup-all-agents` (same as Linux) | `~/.local/state/one-setup-all-agents` (same as Linux) |
| Override | `ALL_AGENTS_CONFIG_DIR` or `--config-dir` | `ALL_AGENTS_STATE_DIR` |

Rules:

- The command line flag beats the environment variable, which beats the default.
- State is never inside the config directory. The config directory is meant to be copied, versioned or shared between machines; the state holds absolute paths and backups that only make sense on one machine.
- The state directory is created with mode `0700` on POSIX and its files with `0600`, because backups contain copies of the tools' config files, which may hold secrets. Backup contents are never printed.
- The engine receives both directories through `Env` (`model.py`). No other code computes them.
- Tool config roots (where Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Antigravity keep their files) are not decided here. Each adapter's `paths()` owns them and must honor that tool's own override variables.

## Reason

- Separating source from state makes the source portable and keeps secrets-bearing backups out of anything a user might commit.
- XDG paths are the Linux convention. The AI tools this project manages already use `~/.config`-style and dotfolder locations on every OS, so macOS follows Linux rather than `~/Library/Application Support`.

## Open points

- macOS: `~/.config` and `~/.local/state`, same as Linux (decided). `~/Library/Application Support` is not used.
- WSL and Windows have separate homes and therefore separate configs. Sharing one config between them is possible by pointing `ALL_AGENTS_CONFIG_DIR` at the same folder; the documentation must say so. Not tested.
- GUI apps on macOS do not see shell environment variables, so an override set only in a shell profile is not seen by them. Relevant for secrets by variable name; document it.

# 0003: Source layout on disk

Status: Accepted (MCP source stays JSONC, confirmed by the maintainer)

## Decision

The source of truth is a folder of plain files in the config directory (0002). It is separate from the tool's code: after `pipx install` there is no repository checkout, so nothing in the config may refer to the install location.

```text
<config-dir>/
  config.toml                 version = 1, which tools are enabled
  instructions.md             core instructions, shared by every tool
  instructions.<tool>.md      optional per-tool appendix (claude, codex, opencode, agy)
  mcp.jsonc                   tool-neutral MCP server definitions
  skills/<name>/SKILL.md      one folder per skill
```

- Instructions: each tool receives the core file, plus its own appendix if one exists. The planner checks the rendered size against the tool's limit (Antigravity has one) and reports an overflow instead of writing.
- MCP: neutral fields only (`command`, `args`, `url`, and the names of the environment variables the server needs). The adapter translates to each tool's format. Secrets are referenced by variable name; the file never holds a value.
- Skills: the source of truth for the skills the user wants shared (see 0007).
- `config.toml` has an optional `[projects]` table (`personal_owners`, `personal_paths`) that tells project scope (v0.2) which repositories are yours; with no configuration every project counts as a team project, the safe default.
- `config.toml` carries `version = 1` so the format can change later; an unknown version is refused, not guessed.
- `all-agents init` creates this layout by importing what the tools already contain, after a full safety snapshot (0005).
- Reading all of this needs only the standard library: TOML via `tomllib`, JSONC via a small reader in the project.

## Reason

- Files the user can read, edit and keep under version control build trust; there is nothing hidden to migrate.
- A core file plus optional per-tool appendix covers "same rules everywhere, plus one tool-specific note" without templating.
- JSONC for MCP matches what users already hand-write for these tools (comments allowed), and the project needs a JSONC reader anyway to edit OpenCode's config.

## Open points

- MCP source format: JSONC (decided). TOML would have avoided a custom reader for the source but not for OpenCode's config.
- Whether `init` offers a "merge" when several tools have different global instructions (needs interactive choice design in Phase 4).
- Names of the per-tool appendix files if a fifth tool is added (the pattern `instructions.<id>.md` already covers it).

# 0005: One journal, backup and ledger format; the `undo` guarantee

Status: Accepted

## Context

"Any change can be undone with one command" is the product promise and the top risk. A previous prototype of this idea kept four different manifest formats, needed the user to pass a folder path to roll back, refused changed files without a way forward, wrote one tool's config through a non-atomic remove-then-add, and treated links as something other than files. This project has one format for every kind of change.

## Decision

All changes are expressed as the three engine ops (`EditFile`, `RunCli`, `Link`; `Unsupported` is never executed) and recorded in one place.

State directory (0002):

```text
ledger.json                  ownership + index of operations
ops/<op-id>/journal.json     the entries of one operation
ops/<op-id>/files/NNNN       backup payloads referenced by the journal
```

- **Operation id**: UTC timestamp plus a short random suffix, for example `20261106T101500Z-a1b2`. Sortable, unique, no counters.
- **`journal.json`**: `{"format": "one-setup-all-agents/journal", "version": 1, "id", "label", "created", "status", "entries": [...]}`. Status is `open`, `done`, `failed` or `undone`.
- **Entry**: `seq`, `type` (`edit_file`, `run_cli`, `link`), `status` (`planned`, `done`, `failed`), `before` and `after`.
  - `before` and `after` describe a path as one of: `absent`; `file` (sha256, mode, backup reference); `symlink` (target); `dir_link` (kind `junction` or `symlink`, target); `copy_tree` (tree hash, marker).
  - `run_cli` entries carry `argv` and `inverse_argv`. An op without an inverse is rejected at plan time.
- **`ledger.json`**: `{"format": "one-setup-all-agents/ledger", "version": 1, "owned": {tool: {kind: [item keys]}}, "operations": [{id, label, created, status}]}`. `owned` is what lets `sync` touch only entries this tool created, and remove them when they leave the source.
- **Write-ahead**: before an op runs, its entry (with `before` captured and any backup file written and fsynced) is saved with status `planned`. After it runs and is verified, it becomes `done`. A crash therefore leaves a journal that still knows how to put things back.
- **Verification**: after each write the engine re-reads the result and compares it with the expected `after`; a mismatch triggers an automatic revert of the entries already done in this run.
- **Safety snapshot**: `init` first records a `snapshot` operation holding copies of every config file of every detected tool, including those it will not change. `undo` of `init` restores them.
- **Secrets**: backups can contain secrets, so they live in the `0700` state directory, are never printed, and plan or status output goes through a mask.

## The `undo` guarantee (what we promise)

`all-agents undo` reverses the most recent operation that is not undone. After a successful undo, every path that operation changed is back in its recorded `before` state: same bytes, same permission bits, same link-or-file kind. Entries are reversed in the opposite order of execution. The undo is itself an operation in the journal, so it can be undone.

What we do not promise: reverting changes made by other programs after our operation; undoing the side effects of an external CLI beyond running its recorded inverse.

## Drift rules (Accepted)

A path has drifted when its current state differs from the entry's recorded `after`: the tool or the user changed it since.

- `undo` first checks all entries (preflight). If any path has drifted, it changes nothing, lists the drifted paths and exits non-zero.
- `undo --force` proceeds. Before overwriting a drifted path it saves the current content as a new journal operation, so even a forced undo is reversible.

## Undo is a stack (Accepted)

- `undo` reverts only the latest operation that is not undone. Run it again to revert the one before, and so on. There is no way to jump to a chosen operation id.
- `undo --list` shows the operations that can still be undone, newest first. It is informational.
- Reason: operations build on each other. Reverting an older operation directly can break the ones after it (for example a later operation edited the same file or linked into a folder the older one created), and the result is a state no operation ever produced. A stack keeps every intermediate state one that really existed.
- Retention: keep the last 20 operations. Pruning removes the oldest first and never the latest. An operation that was pruned can no longer be undone.

## Reason

- One format means one `undo` path, one test suite for it, and every new adapter inherits the guarantee.
- A preflight check avoids half-undone states, which are worse than none.

## Open points

- Claude Code's MCP config is written through the tool's CLI (`remove` then `add`), which is not atomic. The journal must mark such an entry `partial` if the second step fails, and undo must tolerate a half state. Not designed in detail.
- Whether pruning runs automatically after each `sync` or only on demand (the limit of 20 is decided; the trigger is not).
- Cross-machine use of the journal is out of scope: it holds absolute paths for one machine.
- `copy_tree` before-state for large skill folders: storing a hash plus a copy may be expensive; decide when the skills adapter is built.

# 0006: Atomic writes, permissions and symlinks

Status: Accepted

## Context

A common atomic-write recipe (temporary file, fsync, `os.replace`) is crash-safe but, on POSIX, silently loses the target's permission bits (a `0600` file becomes the umask default) and replaces a symlink with a regular file. Users who keep their dotfiles in a repository and link them into place would have their links destroyed, and a private config could become world-readable. A tool that edits real config files must not do either.

## Decision

All file writes go through `engine/atomic.py`. Adapters never call it (0008).

1. **Same-directory temp file.** Create the temporary file in the real target's directory so `os.replace` stays on one filesystem and is atomic. Never in a system temp directory.
2. **Follow symlinks.** If the target path is a symlink, resolve it and write the real file; the link stays a link. A dangling symlink is an error, not a reason to create the target.
3. **Preserve permissions.** If the target exists, copy its mode bits onto the temp file before the replace. If it does not exist, use the default for new files, and `0600` when the op is marked `sensitive` (files known to hold credentials).
4. **Preserve text conventions.** Keep the existing file's line endings (LF or CRLF) and UTF-8 BOM. Edits are minimal and textual, so comments and formatting survive.
5. **Durability.** Flush and `fsync` the temp file, `os.replace`, then on POSIX `fsync` the directory. Skip the directory fsync on Windows.
6. **Windows.** `os.replace` is atomic on one volume. Retry a few times with a short backoff on `PermissionError`, because antivirus and indexers briefly hold files. Give up with a clear error; do not fall back to a non-atomic write.
7. **Optimistic concurrency.** Immediately before replacing, compare the file's current hash with the op's `expect_sha256`. A mismatch aborts that op (the tool changed the file since planning). A small race window remains and is documented, not hidden.
8. **Verify.** After the replace, re-read and compare with the intended bytes (0005).
9. **Files owned by a running tool** (for example a config file that live sessions also write) are not edited in place; the adapter plans a `RunCli` through the tool's own command instead.
10. **Cleanup.** The temp file is removed on any failure.

## Reason

Each rule closes a specific way an "atomic" write still damages a user's setup. The test suite for `atomic.py` must have one test per rule, run on all three OSes (POSIX-only rules are skipped on Windows, not removed).

## Open points

- Hard links are broken by a replace (the other name keeps the old content). Documented as a limit, not handled.
- Ownership (`chown`), extended attributes and macOS ACLs are not preserved. Unverified whether any supported tool relies on them.
- Behavior when the real target is on a read-only or network filesystem is not specified beyond "fail with a clear error".
- The exact retry count and backoff for Windows are placeholders to tune with real data.

# 0008: Adapter and engine boundary

Status: Accepted

## Decision

- An adapter **detects, reads and plans. It never writes.** It returns `Op` objects. Only `engine/` touches the disk, takes backups, keeps the journal, verifies and undoes.
- The engine executes exactly three kinds of op:
  - `EditFile(path, transform, expect_sha256, ...)`: atomic write with verification and journal (0005, 0006).
  - `RunCli(argv, inverse_argv, ...)`: for files a tool owns itself. The inverse is mandatory.
  - `Link(link, target, ...)`: junction, symlink or copy fallback (0007).
  - Plus `Unsupported(tool, kind, reason)`, which is never executed; it makes a gap visible in the plan as lossy.
- The adapter interface (`adapters/base.py`): `id`, `label`, `capabilities`; `detect`, `paths`; `read_instructions`, `read_mcp`, `read_skills`; `plan_instructions`, `plan_mcp`, `plan_skills`; optional `plan_hooks`, `plan_permissions`, `plan_memory` (default: `Unsupported`); `notes`.
- Adapters receive an explicit `Env` (home, platform, environment, config and state directories). They do not read the OS themselves, which makes them testable on any machine.
- `plan_*` functions are pure. Planning twice, with an apply in between, yields an empty second plan.
- Adapters touch only entries recorded as owned in the ledger.
- One adapter contract test runs against every registered adapter. A tool is not merged until it passes: reading what its plan produces returns the desired state, a second plan is empty, undo restores the original bytes.
- Adapters live in-tree. There is no plugin or entry-point mechanism in v0.x.
- Adapter ids: `claude`, `codex`, `opencode`, `agy`. Module names are descriptive (`claude_code.py`, `antigravity.py`).

## Reason

- Safety and undo are properties of the engine, so they cannot differ per tool. If adapters wrote files, each would need its own backup and rollback; that is how earlier prototypes ended up with seven write paths.
- A new tool becomes one module (about 150 to 300 lines) plus a fixture and a registry line, instead of edits across many files.
- Making unsupported kinds explicit keeps the product honest: a tool that cannot express something says so in the plan.

## Open points

- The exact shape of `desired` and `owned` arguments is a sketch; it will be fixed when the first adapter (OpenCode) is ported, and this ADR updated.
- A third-party adapter mechanism (entry points) is deferred until the interface is stable.
- Whether some tools need an op kind beyond these three (for example an edit that must also restart something) is unknown until Claude Code and Antigravity are ported.

# 0009: Adapter interface v1

Status: Accepted

This settles the open point of 0008 ("the exact shape of `desired` and `owned`") and the gaps found while writing the contract test (`tests/adapter_contract.py`). It changes no rule of 0008: adapters still never write, `plan_*` stays pure, `Env` stays explicit, and hooks, permissions and memory still default to `Unsupported`.

## Decision

**Item keys and `owned`.** Every managed item has a key within its kind: the server name for MCP, the skill name for skills, and the fixed key `instructions` (`INSTRUCTIONS_KEY`) for the instructions file, which is owned as one item. The ledger of 0005 already stores `owned: {tool: {kind: [item keys]}}`. An adapter now receives only its own keys for that kind, as `Owned = frozenset[str]`, in every `plan_*` call. `desired` is a `str` for instructions, `{name: McpServer}` for MCP and a sequence of `SkillRef` (the source folders) for skills.

**Ownership flows back through the ops.** `EditFile`, `RunCli` and `Link` each get two optional fields, `claims` and `releases`: tuples of `ItemRef(tool, kind, key)`. An op lists the items it creates or updates in `claims` and the items it removes in `releases`. The engine updates `owned` from the ops it applied and nothing else. An `ItemRef` carries the tool id, so a flat plan stays self-describing.

**Removal of a link.** `Link.target` may be `None`, meaning "remove this link". Without it a skill that left the source could not be withdrawn (the three executable ops had no removal for a directory link). It applies only to a link, junction or marked copy that the ledger records as owned.

**Conflicts.** A new non-executed op, `Conflict(tool, kind, key, reason, path)`, expresses "this item is in the way or cannot be written, and is left alone". It is used for:

- a destination that exists, is not owned and differs from what is wanted (0007, and the same rule for an MCP entry or the instructions file);
- desired content the tool cannot take, for example instructions over a size limit (0003).

`Unsupported` keeps its meaning ("the tool cannot express this kind"). `Plan.is_empty` is true only when there is nothing to run and nothing to report: `Unsupported` entries do not count (a permanent gap), a `Conflict` does (the desired state is not reached and the user must be told). `Plan` also gets `executable` and `conflicts`. So "a second plan after apply is empty" holds when there are no conflicts, and a conflict-only plan is not empty and has nothing to execute. An existing item that is not owned but already equals the wanted state produces neither an op nor a conflict.

**Normalization.** A tool may legitimately lose information, so "reading what the plan produced gives back `desired`" means "gives back `normalize(desired)`". `ToolAdapter` gets two overridable methods, `normalize_instructions(text)` and `normalize_mcp(servers)`, both identity by default. An adapter overrides one only for the fields its format cannot store; the contract test uses it as the expected value. Skills have no normalizer: they are compared by name and link target.

**`McpServer` fields.** The type is extended with what the neutral source (`_core/source.py`, `tests/fixtures/servers.jsonc`) needs and a tool can carry: `headers` (a tuple of `HeaderRef(name, env_var, scheme)`, the value always coming from an environment variable, for example `Authorization: Bearer ${TOKEN}`), `cwd`, `auth` (`None`, `oauth` or `none`), `enabled` and `startup_timeout_sec`; `transport` is derived (`http` when `url` is set). `env_vars` stays a tuple of variable NAMES that the tool passes on from its own environment. Non-secret literal values are carried by a new field `env: tuple[tuple[str, str], ...]`, sorted by name so that equality and hashing are stable (a plain mapping would be unhashable inside a frozen dataclass and order-dependent). A value is rejected with `ValueError` at construction when it looks like a secret, using the one check the legacy source also uses (`env_value_looks_secret` in `_core/mask.py`: masking would change the value, or the name sounds secret and the value is not just a reference such as `${VAR}`); a name may not appear in both `env` and `env_vars`, or twice in `env`. So no adapter can carry a secret value, and the rule that secrets are referenced by variable name only still holds: `env` is for values such as `MODE=test`. Header values stay variable-only (`HeaderRef`). The source-level selectors `tools`, `keep_live_env` and `description` are not part of the type: choosing which tools get a server is the engine's job, not an adapter's.

**Contract test.** `tests/adapter_contract.py` is a reusable mixin that runs the checks of 0008 against any adapter in a temporary home, and `tests/test_adapter_contract.py` applies it to a neutral example adapter, to deliberately broken adapters and to every registered adapter (a visible skip while the adapter is still a `StubAdapter`). Ops are applied by a test-only stand-in (`tests/contract_applier.py`, one function as the seam, `make_applier`).

## Reason

- The engine cannot keep the ledger or let `sync` remove entries unless ops say which items they create and remove; guessing it from paths would put tool knowledge into the engine.
- A frozenset of keys is the smallest type that is exact: an adapter cannot be handed the ledger of another tool or kind by mistake.
- 0007 and 0003 already require "report, do not write". Mapping that onto `Unsupported` would blur "cannot express" with "will not touch", and mapping it onto an executable op would break the rule that the plan shows exactly what runs.
- A conflict-only plan reading as empty would let `sync` say "nothing to do" while the user's tools differ from the source.
- Without `normalize_*`, the round-trip check either fails for every adapter that loses a field, or is weakened until it proves nothing.
- Headers and `cwd` appear in the real source and the fixture; a model that cannot hold them would force an adapter to read the raw source, which breaks the boundary.

## Open points

- The contract test's undo check runs against a stand-in, not `engine/`. The `undo` guarantee of 0005 is NOT proven by it. It becomes real only when `make_applier` returns the real engine and the whole suite passes. This is the next plan item.
- Ownership changes that need no op have no carrier: adopting an existing item that already equals the wanted state, and dropping an owned item that has already vanished. The assumption is that `init` (which imports existing config into the source) and the engine's ledger reconciliation record these directly. To be confirmed when the engine is built.
- Literal header values are not representable. The literal-env design does not cover them cleanly: the source judges headers with a different rule (the header name decides, `Authorization` and similar must be references) and they need their own field. Decide when an adapter needs one.
- The copy-plus-manifest fallback of 0007 (`Link.allow_copy_fallback`) is not exercised by the stand-in; links are always plain links there.
- `RunCli` sequences such as "remove, then add" are not atomic (0005 open point); the contract suite applies them step by step and does not simulate a failure between the two.
- `desired` for hooks, permissions and memory is still `object`; it is fixed when those kinds get an implementation.
- Project scope (v0.2) is not covered by the contract test; it runs `Scope.GLOBAL` only.
- A third-party adapter mechanism stays deferred, as in 0008.

# 0010: Engine v1

Status: Accepted

This records the choices made while building `engine/` (plan item "Build the unified engine"): one operation model, one journal for backup and ledger, automatic revert when a write fails. It changes no rule of 0002, 0005, 0006, 0007, 0008 or 0009. Where it settles an open point of an accepted ADR, it says so. The legacy formats in `_core/` are not wired to this engine and stay until the adapters are ported, so "one journal instead of four formats" is true for the new engine only.

## Decision

**Journal and ledger (0005).**

- Layout and ids exactly as in 0005. Every journal and ledger file is written with `engine/atomic.py` (`0600` in `0700` folders on POSIX; an existing state directory is tightened to `0700`). On Windows no ACL is set: the folder inherits the user profile's.
- A path is described by a state dict with a `state` key: `absent`; `file` (`sha256`, `mode`); `symlink` (`target`); `dir_link` (`kind` `junction` or `symlink`, `target`); `copy_tree` (`tree_sha256`, `marker`). A before-state of a file or copied tree also has `backup` (`files/NNNN`); a copied tree has `modes` too.
- Entry fields beyond 0005: `description` (masked), `path`, `real_path` (an edit through a symlink changes the real file and leaves the link), `claims`, `releases`, `created_dirs` (folders the op created, removed again on revert when empty, so an undo leaves no new folders behind), `effect: "none"` (the atomic write was refused, nothing changed), `expected_after` (when verification failed), `result` (`exit_code`, for `run_cli`), `error` (masked), `reverted`. A `run_cli` entry has `before` and `after` of `null`: it has no path.
- Operation fields beyond 0005: `owned_delta`, `pending_revert`, `recovered`, `error`.
- Write-ahead order per op: capture `before`, write and fsync the backup payload, save the entry as `planned` (with the expected `after` computed up front: the transform is pure), execute, observe, compare, save `done`. The copy fallback saves the entry again before it starts, because the expected `after` changes from a link to a copy.
- Ownership: `owned` is updated only at the end of a successful run, from the ops that ran. The delta (`added`, `removed` triples) is saved in the journal first, then the ledger is written, then the operation is marked `done`. A revert applies the delta backwards, as set arithmetic: it is exact (an item already owned before a claim stays owned) and safe to repeat after a crash. A failed run never reaches the ledger.
- `apply_plan(env, plan, *, label, run_cli=None, lock_timeout=0.0)` returns the operation id, or `None` (nothing recorded) when the plan has nothing executable. Errors: `EngineLockedError`, `OpenOperationError`, `PlanError` (checked before anything is touched, for example a `RunCli` without an inverse), `ApplyError` (`reverted` says whether the automatic revert finished).

**Lock.** An operating-system lock on `<state>/lock`: `fcntl.flock(LOCK_EX | LOCK_NB)` on POSIX, `msvcrt.locking(LK_NBLCK, 1)` on Windows. It fails at once with `EngineLockedError` naming the holder (or after `timeout` seconds), never waits forever. A stale lock cannot exist, because the OS drops the lock when the process ends, however it ends; the pid line in the file is informational (it sits after the locked byte so other processes can read it) and is overwritten by the next holder. A crashed run is not a lock problem; it is an `open` operation (below). Resolves the plan wording "stale lock handling".

**Junction (resolves the open point of 0007).** `_winapi.CreateJunction` is the method: in-process, no quoting, no subprocess, no administrator rights. It is undocumented in the standard library, so if the interpreter lacks it the same junction is made with `mklink /J` through `cmd.exe` (argv list). Both paths are tested on Windows. Linux and macOS use a symlink with an absolute target. Tested here on CPython 3.14 only; the CI matrix must cover 3.11 to 3.13.

**Links.**

- Something already at the link path is replaced or removed only if it is a link, junction or marked copy and the ledger records an item of the op as owned: removal needs `releases` and every released item owned; replacement needs at least one of `claims` and `releases` owned. A regular file, a real folder without a marker, and anything unowned are never touched. A marked copy whose content no longer matches its marker is refused (the user's edits would be lost). A path already in the wanted state is a no-op.
- The fallback (`allow_copy_fallback`) copies the folder next to the destination, writes the marker (`.all-agents-copy.json`: `source`, `tree_sha256`), and renames the copy into place, so the destination is absent or whole. Without the flag a link failure is an error and leaves nothing.
- Copy-tree hashing cost: the tree hash is a SHA-256 over sorted names and every file's bytes, streamed; the marker is excluded; modes are not hashed (they are stored in the before-state and restored). It is computed at capture, after the copy, and at each drift check. A before-state copied tree is stored as a full copy in the payload. This is accepted because copied trees exist only for the fallback and skill folders are small; a tree above 64 MiB or 5000 files, or one containing a link, is refused up front. Resolves the open point of 0005 and the hash rule of 0007.

**RunCli.**

- Executed through a runner, `argv -> exit code`. The default uses `subprocess.run` with an argv list, never `shell=True`, `shutil.which` to find the program (so a Windows `.cmd` shim works), a 120 s timeout, output captured and discarded, 127 for a missing program. Tests inject a fake and never start a program.
- "Verified" means: the runner returned 0. The engine cannot re-read a file it does not know, so there is no stronger check at this level; an adapter's own `read_*` after the apply is the stronger check, and the contract suite does it. The same holds for the inverse on a revert.
- The journal keeps `argv` in clear (the revert needs it); the folder is private. Everything the engine prints or raises goes through the mask, and shows at most the first three arguments.
- Revert of a `run_cli` entry: `done` runs its inverse (a failure stops the revert); `failed` with a non-zero exit code is not inverted (the command reported failure, so it is assumed to have had no effect); `planned`, or `failed` without an exit code, has an unknown outcome, so the inverse is tried and a failing inverse is tolerated and noted (`revert_note`).
- A remove-then-add pair (the 0005 open point): if the add fails, the add is not inverted and the remove is, which re-adds the old entry; the run is `failed` and the ledger is unchanged. No `partial` status is needed. If the inverse of the remove also fails, the operation stays `failed` with `pending_revert` and the journal shows which entries are put back. Resolves that open point.

**Crash recovery.** A crash leaves the operation `open` (or `failed` with `pending_revert` if an automatic revert was interrupted). The next `apply_plan` refuses with `OpenOperationError` and points at `apply.recover_operation(env)`, which reverts each such operation, newest first, and marks it `failed`, `recovered`. A `planned` entry may or may not have executed, so recovery accepts the path being in the `before` state, the expected `after` state, or (for a link, which is replaced in two steps) absent. Anything else is drift.

**Revert (`revert.revert_operation(env, op_id, *, run_cli=None, lock_timeout=0.0)`).** Takes the lock. Works on `done` (becomes `undone`), `open` and `failed` with `pending_revert` (become `failed`). Drift preflight is the only mode: if any path of an entry still to be reverted is in a state other than the recorded `after` (or `before`), nothing is changed and `RevertError` lists the paths. Entries are reversed newest first and marked `reverted` as they go, so an interrupted revert resumes. Restore replaces the path through `atomic.py` with the recorded mode, then checks the result. Not built, and not made harder: `--force`, the stack rule, `--list`, retention of 20, and recording the undo as an operation of its own (0005 says an undo is an operation; here it only sets the target to `undone`).

**Planning.** `build_plan(env, adapters, desired, *, scope=GLOBAL, kinds=None)`: `desired` is a `DesiredState` (`instructions`, `mcp`, `skills`, and `hooks`, `permissions`, `memory`) applied to every adapter, or a mapping of adapter id to `DesiredState` (per-tool selection of servers is the engine's job per 0009). `None` for a core kind means "not managed": it is skipped. The optional kinds are always asked so that `Unsupported` shows. `owned` per tool and kind is read from the ledger. The source loader for the config directory is not part of this item. `merge_links` collapses `Link` ops with the same path (0007): same target or both removals give one op with the claims and releases of all adapters (`allow_copy_fallback` stays on only if all allow it); a removal against a link keeps the link and moves the `releases` onto it (another tool still wants it); different targets keep the first and report a `Conflict`. `render_plan` prints what would run, then conflicts and unsupported kinds; file contents are never shown; every line goes through the mask, and an argument that is a JSON document is masked field by field.

**What the contract suite proves (0009 open point).** `tests/contract_applier.make_applier` returns the real engine. A pass shows, for the neutral example adapters in a temporary home: every apply is journaled and undone to the exact files, folders, links and `owned` table it started from; entries of the user and unowned entries are untouched; a conflict changes nothing. Run on Windows (junctions) and on Linux (symlinks, `0700`/`0600`, `flock`) through WSL, CPython 3.14. Not proven: macOS (CI only); CPython 3.11 to 3.13; any real tool (where it keeps files, whether it follows links, what its CLI does); the `undo` command (Phase 5); a crash at an arbitrary instruction (crashes are simulated at the points of the write-ahead order); Windows file symlinks; behavior on network filesystems.

## Reason

- Each choice closes a way an apply could leave a setup half changed or an undo could destroy the user's data: write-ahead plus recovery for crashes, drift preflight for third-party edits, ownership checks for links, the delta for the ledger.
- An OS lock needs no cleanup and has no stale state; a pid file needs liveness probing that differs per OS.
- `_winapi.CreateJunction` avoids spawning `cmd.exe` per skill and its quoting rules; the fallback costs one function.
- Exit code 0 is the only result every CLI offers; claiming more would be a guess.

## Open points

- Advisory locks on NFS or SMB are unverified; the state directory is machine-local by design.
- macOS, and CPython 3.11 to 3.13, are not run here.
- Windows ACLs on the state directory are not set.
- Backups are never pruned yet; retention of 20 is Phase 5.
- A link replace is two steps (remove, create), not atomic; recovery handles it, but a POSIX rename-into-place could remove the window.
- A hard crash during a copy can leave a `.all-agents-tmp-*` sibling folder; recovery does not delete it.
- A `RunCli` has no drift check, and an uncertain one (a crash) is resolved by trying its inverse.
- Two adapters editing the same file are not merged; only links are.
- `RunCli` verification is weak by nature; a per-op read-back hook is possible later.
- Adoption of an existing equal item into `owned` (0009 open point) is still without a carrier; `journal.set_owned` is the low-level function `init` can use.
- An op list that edits a path and also links over it is not analysed; ops run in order.

# 0011: Claude Code adapter

Status: Accepted

This records the choices made while porting the Claude Code adapter (`adapters/claude_code.py`). It changes no rule of 0005 to 0010. Where it settles an open point of an accepted ADR, it says so. Facts marked [docs] come from the official Claude Code documentation, [prototype] from the legacy implementation this project grew out of (ported in `_core/`), and [unverified] were not checked against a live tool.

## Decision

**Paths (global scope).** `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` is read from `env.environ`, never from the OS, and only when it is an absolute path in the style of `env.platform`. A relative, `~` or foreign-style value is ignored, and `detect()` warns, because Claude Code would resolve a relative value against its own working directory, which an adapter cannot know.

| Item | With `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=<d>` | Without |
|---|---|---|
| Instructions | `<d>/CLAUDE.md` | `<home>/.claude/CLAUDE.md` |
| Skills | `<d>/skills/<name>` | `<home>/.claude/skills/<name>` |
| MCP (user scope) | `<d>/.claude.json` | `<home>/.claude.json` |

[docs] state that with the variable set, Claude Code reads `.claude.json` from inside that directory instead of from the home directory. The default locations are [prototype] verified on Windows. The effect of the variable with a live tool, and everything on Linux and macOS, is [unverified].

**MCP is written through the CLI, not by editing `.claude.json` (settles the 0005 open point for this tool).** Claude Code rewrites `.claude.json` constantly (counters, per-project state, caches). An `EditFile` would be refused by the engine's content check whenever a session wrote in between, and a read-modify-write of the whole file could lose that session's changes. The CLI writes with Claude Code's own logic. So `plan_mcp` returns `RunCli` ops, always with `-s user` (a same-named project or local server is never touched):

| Change | `argv` | `inverse_argv` |
|---|---|---|
| add | `claude mcp add-json <name> '<json>' -s user` | `claude mcp remove <name> -s user` |
| remove | `claude mcp remove <name> -s user` | `claude mcp add-json <name> '<old entry>' -s user` |
| change an owned server | the remove, then the add | as above |

The CLI has no update, so a change is two ops, and the engine's revert of a failed add re-adds the old entry (0010, "A remove-then-add pair"). The file is only read, to compare, with one retry for a torn read. Keys of an owned entry that the adapter does not own (`oauth`, `headersHelper`, ...) are carried into the re-added entry. The old entry goes into `inverse_argv` and a patched copy into `argv`, which means into the journal in clear and onto a process command line. So before a remove or a replace of an owned entry, every nested string of the old entry (env values with their keys, header values, `oauth` fields, arguments after a secret-looking flag) is checked with the `_core/mask.py` detectors; a `${NAME}` reference is fine. If anything looks secret, no `RunCli` is planned for that server: it is a `Conflict` that names the field, never the value, and says to move the value to an environment variable or edit the entry by hand.

The binary is `ALL_AGENTS_CLAUDE_BIN` (a path, the prototype's variable; a path that does not exist is reported, not replaced by a different install found on `PATH`), else `claude` on the `PATH` of `env.environ`. If it is missing, each server that would change becomes a `Conflict` that says so, and the instructions and skills of the same tool are unaffected. A plan with nothing to change needs no CLI. On Windows, a `claude.cmd` shim (the npm install) re-parses its arguments in `cmd.exe`, so an argument with one of `% & | < > ^ !` is refused with a `Conflict` instead of being passed; `claude.exe` has no such limit.

**Entry format.** `{"type": "stdio", "command", "args", "env"}` and `{"type": "http", "url", "headers"}`. `type` is always written (an entry with a `url` and no `type` is a configuration error [docs]). A secret is `${NAME}` (Claude Code expands `${VAR}` and `${VAR:-default}` in `command`, `args`, `env`, `url` and `headers` [docs]); a header is `Scheme ${NAME}`. Reading accepts `sse` and `streamable-http` as http, skips a `ws` entry, never copies a secret-looking literal or a reference to a differently named variable into the neutral model, and strips a `.cmd` suffix from `npx`, `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn`. "Equal" means equal on the keys the adapter owns, with defaults filled in, so a user's equal entry with extra keys or no `type` is left alone.

**Not representable, so `Unsupported` (never silent):**

- `cwd`: not a documented key [docs]. The prototype wrote it; whether Claude Code honors it is [unverified], so it stays unsupported until a documented key exists.
- `startup_timeout_sec`: Claude Code has only the global `MCP_TIMEOUT`.
- For an http server: `command`, `args`, `env`, `env_vars`, `cwd`. For a stdio server: `headers`.
- `auth`: documentation only; OAuth is the default.
- Not written at all, with a reason: a server name the CLI rejects (only letters, digits, hyphen and underscore, not starting with a hyphen), an env literal containing `${` (Claude Code would expand it), an invalid variable, header or scheme name.

`normalize_mcp` lists exactly what does not survive a round trip.

**A disabled server is not written (`enabled = false`).** The user scope has no per-server switch [docs] (disabling is a per-project list), and the prototype's `disabled` key has no documented effect. Writing the server would turn on something the source disables, so a desired server with `enabled = false` means "should not be present in Claude Code": absent, nothing is planned; present and owned, it is removed by the normal remove path (with a `release`, and with the secret-value refusal above); present and not owned, it is left alone, with no `Conflict` just for being disabled. In every case one `Unsupported` line names the server ("disabled in the source; Claude Code has no per-server switch, so it is not written"). `normalize_mcp` leaves such a server out. The contract suite got a hook, `AdapterContract.unwritten_mcp()`, so an adapter can declare the harness server names it deliberately does not write (`demo-off` for this adapter); nothing else may be dropped.

**Windows launchers.** `npx`, `npm`, `pnpm` and `yarn` are written as plain names on every platform. The prototype did exactly this for Claude Code ("Windows resolves these only as `.cmd` outside Claude Code") and ran it live, and the Claude Code changelog removed its "requires a `cmd /c` wrapper" warning as a false positive [docs]. This differs from the OpenCode adapter, which writes `.cmd` on Windows. Not re-verified here with a live tool.

**Skills.** One `Link` per skill straight from `<config-dir>/skills/<name>` (the source) into `<claude config>/skills/<name>`, with the copy fallback of 0007. Claude Code does not read `~/.agents/skills` [docs, prototype]. The prototype's chain `repo -> ~/.agents/skills -> ~/.claude/skills` is therefore not reproduced: there is no intermediate folder. Skill exclusion is decided but not built: a per-tool exclude list in `config.toml` (the prototype's `claude_exclude`), applied by the loader before the desired skills reach the adapter, so the adapter needs no knob; an owned skill that falls out of the list is withdrawn like any other. Future work for the loader (Phase 4/5). The folders `.trash` and `synced` (managed by Claude Code and claude.ai) are not listed by `read_skills` and are never touched. Symlinks and junctions are followed on Windows [prototype]; Linux and macOS are [unverified] (0007 open point).

**Shared code.** The whole-file instructions rule and the per-skill link planner are identical for OpenCode and Claude Code and live in `adapters/_common.py`. OpenCode's behavior and tests are unchanged.

## Reason

- The CLI route is the only one that is correct while a session is running, and it is the behavior that was used daily in the prototype.
- A plan that says "not stored" for each lost field keeps the product honest (0008); writing an undocumented key to make a round trip look clean would not.
- Refusing a `.cmd` shim with risky characters is cheaper than debugging a mangled server entry.

## Consequences accepted by the maintainer

- **Undo is by inverse command, not by bytes.** Undoing an MCP change runs the recorded inverse (`remove`, or `add-json` with the old entry). The servers are restored; the bytes of `.claude.json` may differ afterwards, because the real CLI may reformat the file and order servers differently. The contract suite checks exact bytes only because its fake CLI writes a canonical form.
- **The prototype's links are adopted by `init` (Phase 4).** Existing junctions `~/.claude/skills/<name> -> ~/.agents/skills/<name>` are not owned and differ from the source, so until then they are reported as `Conflict`. `init` adopts them into ownership. Skills installed by other means into `~/.agents/skills` no longer reach Claude Code unless they are in the source.
- **`cwd` stays unsupported** (above) and **skill exclusion lives in the loader** (above).

## Open points

- **A `RunCli` has no drift check (0010).** An entry changed by a session between the plan and the apply is removed and re-added from the planned view. The window is small; an `add` of a name that appeared meanwhile fails and is reverted.
- **Unverified with a live tool:** Windows launcher names without `.cmd`, `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, symlinks on Linux and macOS, and everything on macOS.
- The version of the `claude` CLI is not read (`detect()` must not start a program). (Since 0014 the version IS read: the adapter declares `version_probe` and only `detect.py` runs it; `detect()` itself still starts no program.)
- The secret-value refusal uses the project's heuristics, so an owned entry with a long opaque argument can be refused without holding a secret; the user then edits it by hand.

# 0012: Codex adapter and shared skill links

Status: Accepted (the maintainer accepted the recommendation on each open point below)

This records the choices made while porting the Codex adapter (`adapters/codex.py`) and while fixing a bug in how the engine merges skill links that two tools share. It changes no rule of 0005 to 0011. Where it settles an open point of an accepted ADR, it says so. Facts marked [docs] come from the Codex source and documentation (read through the `context7` index of the `openai/codex` repository), [prototype] from the legacy implementation this project grew out of (ported in `_core/`), and [unverified] were not checked against a live tool.

## Decision

### Part A: the Codex adapter

**Paths (global scope).** `CODEX_HOME` is read from `env.environ`, never from the OS, and only when it is an absolute path in the style of `env.platform`. An empty, relative, `~` or foreign-style value is ignored, and `detect()` warns about a non-empty one (Codex would resolve a relative value against its own working directory, which an adapter cannot know). `detect()` also warns when an absolute `CODEX_HOME` points to a folder that does not exist, because Codex refuses to start then [docs: `find_codex_home`].

| Item | With `CODEX_HOME=<d>` | Without |
|---|---|---|
| Instructions | `<d>/AGENTS.md` | `<home>/.codex/AGENTS.md` |
| MCP | `<d>/config.toml` | `<home>/.codex/config.toml` |
| Skills | `<home>/.agents/skills/<name>` | `<home>/.agents/skills/<name>` |

Skills do not follow `CODEX_HOME`: Codex reads `<home>/.agents/skills` (and the deprecated `$CODEX_HOME/skills`, which this adapter does not manage) [docs: `ext/skills/src/host_roots.rs`]. That is the folder the OpenCode adapter links into, so a skill is linked once for both tools. [Windows default paths: prototype; the effect of `CODEX_HOME` on Linux and macOS and symlink-following there: unverified.]

**Instructions and `AGENTS.override.md`.** The global file is `<codex home>/AGENTS.md`, owned as one item (shared rule in `_common.py`). Codex reads `AGENTS.override.md` in the same folder instead of `AGENTS.md` when it is not empty [docs]. Then the instructions this adapter writes are not in effect, so `plan_instructions` adds a `Conflict` for the override file (it is never touched; the `AGENTS.md` is still written, ready for when the override is gone) and `detect()` warns. The 32 KiB limit does not apply to the global file [prototype, measured with `codex debug prompt-input`], so no size check is made.

**MCP is edited in `config.toml` as text, through `_core/toml_edit.py`.** Only `[mcp_servers.<name>]` tables are touched. A table that is new or changes is written inside the managed region at the end of the file (`# >>> one-setup-all-agents >>>` ... `# <<< one-setup-all-agents <<<`); an owned table that leaves the source is removed wherever it is; everything else (other tables, comments, key order, BOM, CRLF) is kept. A table that changes loses the comments that were inside it, and moves into the region. The op is an `EditFile` with `expect_sha256` and a pure transform. At plan time the transform is tried on the exact bytes it will receive, and the result is parsed back (`tomllib`) and compared: nothing outside the touched servers may differ, and every touched server must read back as planned. If that fails (the file does not parse, a bare `[mcp_servers]` table, a server defined as an inline table or by dotted keys, nested tables below an owned server) every affected server becomes a `Conflict` with a reason that holds no file content, and nothing is written. An unparseable file gives one `Conflict` per desired or owned server. This is the CLI-free route: unlike `.claude.json`, `config.toml` is not rewritten by a running Codex session while it works, so the content check at apply time is the right drift guard.

**Entry format.** All keys are in `mcp_types.rs` [docs]: stdio `command`, `args`, `env` (literal values), `env_vars` (names Codex passes on; plain names or `{name, source}` tables), `cwd`; http `url`, `bearer_token_env_var`, `http_headers` (literal), `env_http_headers` (header name to variable name); shared `enabled`, `startup_timeout_sec` (seconds, fractions allowed), `tool_timeout_sec`.

| Neutral field | Codex |
|---|---|
| `env_vars` | `env_vars = ["NAME"]` |
| `env` (non-secret literal) | `[mcp_servers.<n>.env]` |
| `HeaderRef("Authorization", V, "Bearer")` | `bearer_token_env_var = "V"` (Codex adds `Bearer `) |
| `HeaderRef(H, V, None)` | `[mcp_servers.<n>.env_http_headers]` with `H = "V"` |
| `enabled = False` | `enabled = false` (native; nothing is "unwritten") |
| `startup_timeout_sec` | `startup_timeout_sec` (native) |

A secret is therefore always a variable NAME, in Codex's own way, and nothing in `env` or `args` is expanded by Codex, so a `${NAME}` there would only be a literal. A header that is neither a whole variable nor `Authorization: Bearer <variable>` (another scheme, or a scheme on another header) cannot be stored: the server is "not written" with a reason (the prototype did the same). A literal `http_headers` table of the user's is not part of the neutral model; it is not read and not touched.

**Which keys are ours.** `command`, `args`, `url`, `env`, `env_vars`, `cwd`, `enabled`, `bearer_token_env_var`, `env_http_headers`, and `startup_timeout_sec` only when the source sets one.
